newsitem.title: UK: ED&F Man details cocoa forecasts.
newsitem.headline: ED&F Man details cocoa forecasts.

text.p: ED&F Man cut its 1996/97 cocoa deficit forecast on Thursday.
"Our estimate for this season's deficit has been reduced since our last report," it said in its May report. "We are now expecting a deficit of 125-150,000 tonnes."

On the production side, the firm said "world cocoa bean production is expected to fall by seven percent in 1996/97 to 2,688,000 tonnes." That figure is down from its current estimate for last year's crop of 2,882,000 tonnes.
Indonesia's record cocoa bean exports were highlighted, and the firm said it expected 1996/97 production there to jump 18 percent to 330,000 tonnes.
In contrast, Brazil's crop will be the lowest in nearly 30 years despite improving "prospects for the tail of the temporao," it said.

ED&F Man also noted West African arrivals have been lower than last season. It estimated Ivory Coast arrivals were currently about 70,000 tonnes lower than last year and Ghana purchases were down 50,000 tonnes.
On consumption, the firm predicted 1995/96 world grindings up 6.2 percent at 2,694,000 tonnes.
It said the increase reflected "strong consumption growth in all markets" although it noted "so far this season, consumption growth appears to have slowed in western Europe."
For 1996/97, it forecasts three- to four-percent grindings growth to 2,795,000 tonnes. It expected most of the extra grind will occur at origin, particularly in West Africa and Asia.

It also noted "recently, major manufacturers have been adding to their forward cover while small- and medium-sized manufacturers have been reducing cover. This latter group is most vulnerable to speculative and fundamental changes."
ED&F Man forecasts world cocoa stocks to drop to 1,085,000 tonnes at the end of the season and the ratio of stocks to consumption to fall to 39 percent.

It said this year's deficit developed despite favourable weather in the major producing countries and said "unless the weather in West Africa improves, the cocoa market faces a substantial drawdown in stocks in 1997/98."
ED&F Man also noted that "due to unfavourable weather, early setting for the new crops in West Africa has been the lowest since 1983."
